one_liner: Single-threaded ~200-line C TCP echo server on liburing, benchmarked in 2020 against the same author's minimal epoll echo server.
what_it_does: This is a demo program, not a library. It is one C file (219 lines on master, 201 on the benchmarked branch) that listens on a port and echoes each received chunk back, driving accept/recv/send entirely through io_uring. There is no API to call: you read it or copy it as a skeleton. It is meant to be run against frevib/epoll-echo-server (124 lines of C) with the rust_echo_bench load generator as a controlled io_uring-vs-epoll comparison.
how_it_is_fast: The epoll server calls epoll_wait and then does one recv() and one send() syscall per ready socket. The io_uring server queues accept/recv/send SQEs and submits a whole batch with one io_uring_enter per loop iteration; an strace in issue #8 shows about 60 SQEs submitted per call. It relies on IORING_FEAT_FAST_POLL: a recv on a socket with no data stays pending in the kernel and completes when data arrives, so the loop issues no separate poll requests (README v1.5: 'Remove all polling'). Master also switched to kernel-selected provided buffers (IORING_OP_PROVIDE_BUFFERS), which adds an extra provide-buffers SQE per message; the author says this lowered throughput, and the published numbers are from the earlier per-fd-buffer branch.
when_to_use: Learning io_uring networking: a short, readable reference for an accept/recv/send completion loop, packing state into the 64-bit user_data, and provided buffers.

As the starting point for your own epoll-vs-io_uring A/B test on your own kernel and hardware, using the paired epoll-echo-server and rust_echo_bench. Plan to re-measure rather than trust the 2020 numbers.

Checking whether syscall batching helps a single-core ping-pong workload with hundreds of concurrent connections and small (128-1000 B) messages. That is where the 2020 page showed the gap (about 1.4-1.6x at 150-1000 clients), with no gain at 1 client.
Linux 5.7+ hosts only. Master exits at startup if IORING_FEAT_FAST_POLL or IORING_OP_PROVIDE_BUFFERS is missing.
when_not_to_use: Production serving. The author calls it 'only a bare minimum show case for io_uring... don't expect production-grade stability' (issue #17). It does not handle short sends, never checks io_uring_get_sqe for NULL, and calls exit(1) on -ENOBUFS.

Relying on the claimed speedup. In issue #8 (open since 2020, 26 comments), three independent commenters could not reproduce it. On Linux 5.8 (Fedora Rawhide; a 4-vCPU GCP VM), io_uring was equal to or slower than epoll, e.g. 227k vs 235k req/s, or within about +/-2k req/s with the winner alternating. The author replied that results 'most likely are different now'.

More than about 1000 concurrent clients. Issue #17 reports master crashing every time above 1100 clients on a 16-core AWS instance, and the benchmark page says both servers crash above about 2000 clients.
Multi-core scaling: it uses one thread and one ring with global buffers, and has no multi-threaded or SO_REUSEPORT mode.

As an example of current best-practice io_uring. It predates ring-mapped provided buffers (io_uring_register_buf_ring, Linux 5.19+) and multishot accept/recv (5.19/6.0), so it neither shows nor measures those.

integration.dependencies: liburing: a system install on master (the bundled copy was removed in 2021); the benchmarked io-uring-feat-fast-poll branch bundles its own liburing copy (liburing.spec there says 0.6)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (designated initializers, for-loop declarations); built with $(CC) -Wall -O2 -D_GNU_SOURCE, and no compiler version is documented. Kernel: Linux 5.7+ for master; the benchmark ran on a patched 5.6.0-rc1+ (io_uring-task-poll branch)
integration.platforms: Linux only; no architecture-specific code (the benchmark ran on x86-64)
integration.thread_safety: Single-threaded event loop with global buffer arrays and one ring; multi-threaded use is not supported or documented

gotchas: The published numbers come from the io-uring-feat-fast-poll branch, not master. That branch indexes fixed per-connection buffers and state by fd number (bufs[fd], conns[fd], 4096 slots, no bounds check). It also calls shutdown() but never close() on disconnect, so fds grow without limit until they overrun those arrays. Master fixed the fd leak in PR #14 (2022); the epoll baseline has the same shutdown-without-close pattern.

On the benchmarked branch the listen socket is SOCK_NONBLOCK, so an io_uring accept can complete with -EAGAIN. The code then queues a recv on that negative 'fd', indexing conns[] out of bounds, and re-arms accept. PR #6 (merged into master in 2020) says this caused extra CQEs on every loop and suggests it, plus a small queue, may explain the 'uninterruptible sleep' hang the benchmark page reports. The hang was never resolved.

On master, a read that fails or hits EOF re-provides the buffer ID taken from cqe->flags >> 16 without checking IORING_CQE_F_BUFFER. Buffer 0 can then be handed to two connections at once, and one client receives another's data (issue #23; fix PR #24 unmerged since June 2025).

Issue #9 argues the comparison is not like for like: the epoll server does recv/send serially on one thread, while io_uring SQEs may run concurrently on kernel iou-wrk worker threads. The page reports only req/s, not the total CPU used by either server.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only to study raw liburing socket calls in about 200 lines, or to seed a controlled io_uring-vs-epoll experiment. For anything that ships, monoio (Rust, thread-per-core) or PhotonLibOS (C++) are maintained io_uring runtimes with their own benchmarks (monoio vs Tokio/epoll on 4 cores; Photon vs boost::asio).
verified_claims_summary: In February 2020 the io-uring-feat-fast-poll build (gcc -O2, compiler version unstated) served a peak of 216,637 req/s at 300 clients with 128-byte messages, against a peak of 152,561 for the author's epoll server (about 1.4x). At 1000 clients the gap was about 1.6x (173,343 vs 108,380), and at 1 client the two were equal. Each server was pinned to one isolated vCPU in a VMware Ubuntu 18.04 guest (patched Linux 5.6.0-rc1+) on a 6-core 2.6 GHz MacBook Pro. Load came from rust_echo_bench, a thread-per-connection blocking client doing 60-second closed-loop ping-pong runs on the same VM. Independent re-runs on Linux 5.8 in issue #8 did not reproduce the gap.
status_note: Stale: the last commit (2024-01-20) was a small bug fix (PR #20), and the author says the project is 'quite stale' and he will only merge fixes. It is MIT-licensed and small enough to copy as a teaching skeleton, but it is not something to depend on.
